Steps to connect to a DB using JDBC?

- Load the driver. This is automatic since JDBC 4; it used to be Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver").
- Get a Connection from DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pwd) or, better, from a DataSource.
- Create a PreparedStatement.
- Execute it: executeQuery (SELECT returns a ResultSet), executeUpdate (DML returns a row count), execute (anything).
- Process the ResultSet.
- Close the resources with try-with-resources.

What is SQL injection and how to prevent it?

The attacker's input becomes part of the SQL: "... WHERE name='" + input + "'" with input ' OR '1'='1. Prevent it with PreparedStatement parameters (or JPA parameters), allow-list validation, least-privilege DB users, and never concatenating user input into ORDER BY or table names.
What is connection pooling? Why HikariCP?

Opening a DB connection is expensive (TCP, authentication). A pool keeps reusable connections open. HikariCP is Spring Boot's default because it's very fast and lightweight. Key settings: maximumPoolSize (often around 10–20; more isn't better), minimumIdle, connectionTimeout, idleTimeout, maxLifetime (shorter than the DB's wait_timeout), leakDetectionThreshold.
How do you manage transactions in JDBC?

Call con.setAutoCommit(false), run the statements, then con.commit(), or con.rollback() in the catch block. Savepoints: con.setSavepoint() and rollback(sp). Isolation: con.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED).
What is batch processing in JDBC?

addBatch() followed by executeBatch() groups many statements (a single round trip only if the driver supports it). For MySQL, add rewriteBatchedStatements=true to the URL to turn them into a single multi-row INSERT, which is much faster.
ResultSet types and concurrency?

Types: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY (default), TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE, TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE. Concurrency: CONCUR_READ_ONLY, CONCUR_UPDATABLE. For large results, use setFetchSize() to stream rows (with MySQL: Integer.MIN_VALUE or useCursorFetch=true).
JDBC driver types?

Type 1 is the JDBC-ODBC bridge (removed). Type 2 is native-API. Type 3 is network protocol (middleware). Type 4 is a pure Java thin driver that speaks the DB's protocol directly. Almost all modern drivers, including MySQL Connector/J, are Type 4.
JDBC vs JdbcTemplate vs JPA?

Raw JDBC means a lot of boilerplate and checked SQLExceptions. JdbcTemplate handles opening and closing resources, translates exceptions into DataAccessException, and maps rows with RowMapper. Use it for SQL-heavy or reporting code. JPA gives you object mapping, dirty checking and caching, and suits domain-heavy CRUD. Newer options are JdbcClient (Spring 6.1) and jOOQ.
Why was Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") needed, and why not now?

A driver registers itself with DriverManager in a static initialiser, so loading the class was enough. Since JDBC 4, DriverManager uses ServiceLoader to read META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver from each JAR, loading drivers automatically. In some WAR setups class loader visibility still breaks that, and Class.forName works around it. Using a DataSource avoids the matter.
Why doesn't PreparedStatement always prevent SQL injection?

It only protects values bound through setXxx. If you concatenate into the SQL ("... ORDER BY " + input) and then prepare that string, the injection already happened. Placeholders can't stand for table names, columns or sort direction, which leaves concatenation as a temptation there. Use an allow-list that maps input to fixed strings. The same applies to dynamic SQL inside stored procedures and to JPQL string building.
What's the output: ps = "SELECT id FROM t WHERE id IN (?)" with setString(1, "1,2")?

On MySQL, one row: id 1, and no error (tested). The whole string is a single value, and comparing an integer column to '1,2' converts the string to the number 1. You must build one ? per value, or use NamedParameterJdbcTemplate, which expands a collection. For very long lists, use a temporary table or batches of IN clauses.
Are JDBC objects thread-safe? Can I share a Connection?

Don't share one. Even where a driver synchronises internally, a Connection carries one transaction and runs one statement at a time, so two threads' work would mix into one transaction. Statement and ResultSet are not thread-safe. The right design is one connection per unit of work, borrowed from a thread-safe DataSource. JdbcTemplate is safe to share since it has no per-call state.
Why not keep a single Connection in a static field?

All threads would share one transaction and one server thread, so requests would serialise and commits would cross. The DB or a firewall will eventually drop an idle connection, leaving every later call broken. There's no recovery logic. A pool solves all of these.
What's the output: rs.getInt("bonus") when bonus is NULL?

0 (tested). Primitive getters can't represent null. Call rs.wasNull() straight after, or use rs.getObject("bonus", Integer.class), or getBigDecimal, which returns null. In a record with Integer fields, use getObject, since auto-boxing 0 hides the missing value.
What's the difference between execute(), executeQuery() and executeUpdate()?

executeQuery returns a ResultSet and throws for non-SELECT. executeUpdate returns a count and throws if the SQL produces rows. execute runs anything and returns a boolean: true means a ResultSet is ready (getResultSet), false means use getUpdateCount. In a test, execute("SELECT 1") returned true with update count -1, and an UPDATE returned false with count 1. It's for tools running unknown SQL, and procedures returning several results.
Why might an UPDATE return 1 when nothing changed?

Connector/J returns rows found by default, by setting the client "found rows" flag, while MySQL's own default count is rows changed. Setting a column to its current value returned 1 in the test. useAffectedRows=true changes that. This also matters for INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, which reports 1 for an insert and 2 for an update.
How would you load 10 million rows into a table with Java?

- Use a PreparedStatement batch with rewriteBatchedStatements=true, flushing every 1,000 to 5,000 rows and committing per chunk so undo logs and locks stay small.
- Stream the input; don't load it all into a list.
- Keep secondary indexes minimal during the load, or add them afterwards. Foreign key and unique checks cost time.
- For maximum speed use LOAD DATA from a file, though it requires configuration.
- Make it restartable: record the last committed chunk.
- Don't use a single huge transaction: it creates replica lag and a slow rollback on failure.
How would you read and export 10 million rows without running out of memory?

Don't use LIMIT/OFFSET, which gets slower as offset grows. Either stream one query (setFetchSize(Integer.MIN_VALUE) or useCursorFetch=true on MySQL, with a RowCallbackHandler or queryForStream in Spring, closing the stream) and write to the file row by row, or use keyset pagination: WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000. Keyset allows restarts and doesn't hold one connection for hours. For a streaming read, use a replica and set a timeout.
What's the difference between connection pool size and thread pool size?

Threads handle requests; connections are a scarcer resource used for part of each request. If the thread pool (200) is much larger than the connection pool (10), threads queue on getConnection, which is fine provided DB time is short. Set connectionTimeout so they fail fast rather than pile up. A pool as large as the thread pool usually pushes the overload onto the database, which is worse.
Why must maxLifetime be shorter than MySQL's wait_timeout?

The server closes connections idle past wait_timeout (8 hours by default), and firewalls often do so much sooner. If the pool believes a connection is alive, the first use fails with "Communications link failure". Retiring connections earlier, by a margin of at least a few seconds, means Hikari always closes first. keepaliveTime also helps with idle-drop firewalls. A connection in use isn't retired until it's returned.
What happens to session state on a pooled connection?

The physical session lives on, so anything you set without the pool knowing leaks to the next borrower: SET @var, SET time_zone, temp tables, SET sql_mode, and unclosed locks from GET_LOCK. Pools reset only the JDBC-visible properties (autocommit, isolation, read-only, catalog). Use the JDBC setters where they exist, and undo other changes before returning, or set them in connectionInitSql for all connections.
Explain the transaction steps in plain JDBC with an exception after the first update.

With setAutoCommit(false), the first update takes row locks and writes undo records. The exception jumps to catch, rollback() applies undo and releases locks, and the row returns to its original value. Without manual mode, the first update would have committed already, leaving half-finished work. If the catch only handles SQLException, a NullPointerException skips the rollback and it's left to the pool on close.
Does con.rollback() undo everything since the connection opened?

No, only work since the last commit, and it requires autocommit off. Calling it in autocommit mode throws an exception on most drivers. DDL statements in MySQL commit implicitly, so can't be rolled back. Non-transactional engines (MyISAM) and sequences or auto-increment values aren't rolled back: a rolled-back insert left a gap in the ID sequence in a MySQL test.
Batch insert with an error in the middle: what's stored?

It depends. With MySQL Connector/J in autocommit mode, the failing row was skipped and others stored: counts [1, -3, 1] (tested). With continueBatchOnError=false it stops at the first failure. With rewriteBatchedStatements=true the batch is one statement, so one bad row fails the whole chunk. With a transaction and a rollback in the catch, nothing is stored. Always read BatchUpdateException.getUpdateCounts(), and design explicitly.
Statement vs PreparedStatement batch?

Statement.addBatch(sql) can mix different SQL strings, but it still concatenates values. PreparedStatement.addBatch() repeats one SQL with different values. It's safe, and the rewrite optimisation works better on it. For inserts with rewriting, the driver merges VALUES lists. For prepared updates with rewriting, it sends a multi-statement packet.
Which exceptions should a DAO throw?

Generally unchecked ones with a clear message. SQLException leaks implementation detail through every layer, and callers can rarely recover. Keep the cause when wrapping. Convert expected cases into meaningful types, such as a duplicate into EmailAlreadyTaken. With Spring you get DataAccessException by adding @Repository or by using templates. Don't catch and log at every level: you'd get the same error several times.
How would you test JDBC code?

Test real SQL on a real database, because mocks of ResultSet only prove your mock. Use Testcontainers to start the same MySQL version as production. H2 is fast but differs in syntax and locking, so it can pass tests that fail in production. Spring's @JdbcTest slices the context and rolls back after each test. Mock the DAO when testing services.
What's a phantom "Communications link failure" and how do you handle it?

It means that the driver lost the socket: the server restarted, a firewall dropped an idle connection, or a failover happened. Check timeouts first: is maxLifetime under wait_timeout? Is keepaliveTime set? Are connectTimeout and socketTimeout configured? A retry is safe only for idempotent work, as you can't know whether a commit in flight succeeded. For writes, use idempotency keys.
JDBC vs Hibernate: when would you pick plain SQL even in a JPA project?

For bulk operations (a saveAll of a million entities is slow), reporting with window functions and CTEs, and hot paths needing exact SQL. JPA is better for rich aggregates and change tracking. Both can share a transaction in Spring because JpaTransactionManager exposes its connection to JdbcTemplate when the data source is the same. Call EntityManager.flush() first so pending changes reach the DB before your SQL reads them.
Output: what does this print? Statement s = con.createStatement(); ResultSet r1 = s.executeQuery("SELECT 1"); ResultSet r2 = s.executeQuery("SELECT 2"); System.out.println(r1.isClosed());

true (tested). A statement holds at most one open result by default, so re-executing closes the previous one. Nested loops need separate statements. getMoreResults(Statement.KEEP_CURRENT_RESULT) exists for multiple results from one execution, if the driver supports it.
What's the order of closing, and what if you close the connection first?

The correct order is ResultSet, Statement, Connection, the reverse of opening, and try-with-resources does this automatically. Closing a real connection first invalidates its children, so they fail if used. With a pool, closing the connection returns it, and using an old statement after that is dangerous, since it may touch a connection now lent to someone else. Hikari's proxy protects you by rejecting calls on a closed connection.

What's the N+1 problem in JDBC, and how do you fix it?

A loop that runs a query per row: load 100 orders, then a query per order for items, 101 round trips. Fixes: use a JOIN with a ResultSetExtractor that groups rows, or do two queries with WHERE order_id IN (...) and assemble in memory. The second avoids row multiplication when there are several child collections. It's the same problem as in JPA, only more visible.
What's the purpose of ConnectionPoolDataSource and XADataSource?

Both are in javax.sql. ConnectionPoolDataSource is a vendor SPI that hands physical connections to a pool. XADataSource produces connections that can join a distributed transaction (two-phase commit across resources), coordinated by a JTA manager. XA is slow and fragile, so microservices generally use the outbox pattern or sagas.
Design: an audit service must write 5,000 events per second to MySQL. Sketch the JDBC approach.

- Don't insert per request. Put events on a bounded in-process queue, or Kafka if loss is unacceptable.
- One or a few writer threads drain up to N events or wait T milliseconds, then write a batch with rewriting on, in one transaction.
- Keep indexes few, and use a sequential primary key so inserts append to the B+Tree instead of splitting pages.
- Partition by date to allow dropping old data instantly.
- Handle failure: retry with backoff on deadlocks, then send to a dead-letter store; when the queue fills, apply backpressure or sample.
- Give it a separate small pool so that audit writes can't starve user traffic.
Do virtual threads make JDBC faster?

No, each query takes the same time. They increase throughput under concurrency because threads waiting on I/O no longer hold OS threads. The connection pool and the database remain the bottleneck, so a too-small pool now shows up as waits in getConnection(), and a huge pool can overload the DB. 💡 Use recent drivers to avoid synchronized pinning on Java 21.
What is pinning and how does it relate to JDBC drivers?

A virtual thread is pinned when it cannot unmount from its carrier while blocked, notably when blocking inside a synchronized block or native call on Java 21–23. Drivers that guarded socket I/O with synchronized could therefore block carrier threads and kill scalability. Fixes: upgrade the driver and pool, move to Java 24+ where monitors no longer pin in most cases, and check with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads (older JDKs) or JFR.
JDBC vs R2DBC?

JDBC is blocking and universal, with mature drivers and full tooling (JPA, Flyway, JdbcTemplate). R2DBC is a non-blocking reactive API returning Publishers, used with Spring WebFlux and Spring Data R2DBC; it has no JPA, fewer features and a harder debugging model. Choose R2DBC only for a fully reactive stack; otherwise JDBC plus virtual threads is simpler.
Spring Data JDBC vs Spring Data JPA?

Spring Data JDBC maps aggregates directly with SQL: loading an aggregate loads it fully, save() writes immediately, and there is no lazy loading, dirty checking, first-level cache or proxy magic. JPA offers more features (lazy associations, caching, JPQL, cascades) at the cost of complexity such as N+1 queries and LazyInitializationException. Spring Data JDBC suits simpler, well-bounded aggregates.
How do you manage schema changes across environments?

With a migration tool like Flyway or Liquibase: versioned scripts in the repo, applied automatically in order and recorded in a history table, so every environment reaches the same schema. Never modify applied scripts, test migrations in CI against a real database (Testcontainers), and design changes in expand/contract steps so old and new app versions work during a rolling deploy.
How do you route read-only queries to a replica?

Mark transactions with @Transactional(readOnly = true), which calls Connection.setReadOnly(true) and lets Hibernate skip dirty checking. A routing DataSource (Spring's AbstractRoutingDataSource, wrapped in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the decision is made after the transaction flags are set) sends read-only transactions to the replica pool and others to the primary. Remember replication lag: read-your-own-writes flows must hit the primary.
